triage.name: Short bowel syndrome
triage.reason: Malabsorption and diarrhea after massive bowel resection; diagnosis follows from surgical history, nutrition exam and absorption labs.

age.peak: adults after massive bowel resection; also infants after necrotizing enterocolitis

demographics: More common in adults who have had extensive small bowel resection for ischemia, Crohn disease, or trauma
In children, most often follows necrotizing enterocolitis or congenital intestinal anomalies

risk_factors.text: Extensive small bowel resection leaving less than about 200 cm of remaining small intestine
Resection that includes the ileocecal valve
Resection of a large portion of the colon
Underlying Crohn disease requiring repeated bowel resections
Mesenteric ischemia or volvulus causing massive bowel infarction
History of necrotizing enterocolitis in infancy

social_history: Long-term dependence on parenteral nutrition or intravenous fluids
Frequent hospitalizations for dehydration and electrolyte replacement

chief_complaints.text: I have diarrhea all day long
I keep losing weight no matter how much I eat
I feel weak and tired all the time
My belly is swollen and I have a lot of gas

hpi.onset: Gradual after recovery from major bowel surgery, becoming obvious over weeks to months
hpi.duration: Weeks to months after the resection; chronic and persistent
hpi.progression: Diarrhea and weight loss worsen as oral intake increases and the remaining bowel fails to absorb enough; symptoms may partially improve over months to years as the bowel adapts
hpi.location: Generalized abdominal discomfort and bloating; diarrhea is diffuse
hpi.quality: Watery, frequent stools; abdominal cramping and bloating
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; can be life-limiting and require intravenous nutrition
hpi.timing: Worse after meals; frequent stools throughout the day and night

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the legs and feet
Tingling in the hands and feet

pertinent_negatives: Use of antibiotics before symptoms started

argues_against: Bloody diarrhea suggests inflammatory or infectious colitis rather than short bowel syndrome
Urinary symptoms point toward a urinary source rather than malabsorption

atypical.how_it_differs: Infants present with failure to thrive, poor feeding, and dehydration after necrotizing enterocolitis or congenital bowel surgery; diarrhea and weight loss are the main clues.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship to oral intake

atypical.how_it_differs: Older adults may have more severe dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities with less obvious diarrhea because of blunted thirst and comorbidities.
Pregnancy can worsen malabsorption and fluid losses; nausea and vomiting of pregnancy may be mistaken for the underlying condition, and nutritional demands are higher.

general.critical: Lethargic, hypotensive, severely dehydrated, appears toxic

Inspect the temples and facial contours

findings.maneuver: Inspect the oral mucosa and tongue

findings.finding: Mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritoneal signs

Press the dorsum of the foot and lower leg

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the proximal limb muscles
Perform a digital rectal exam and inspect the stool
findings.finding: No gross blood in the stool

findings.maneuver: Assess for rebound tenderness and guarding

labs.caveat: Hyponatremia from sodium and water losses in high-output stoma or diarrhea; can also be dilutional from hypotonic IV fluids.
Hypokalemia from stool and stoma losses; worsens with diarrhea and poor intake.
Hypomagnesemia is common after small bowel resection and can cause cramps, tremor and arrhythmia; low magnesium also makes hypokalemia and hypocalcemia refractory.
Hypophosphatemia from malabsorption and refeeding; can cause weakness and rhabdomyolysis when severe.
Hypocalcemia from vitamin D and fat malabsorption; interpret with albumin and magnesium.
Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate-rich small bowel or stoma losses.
Rises with dehydration and prerenal azotemia; a high BUN/creatinine ratio supports volume depletion.
Creatinine can look falsely low when muscle mass is depleted, so a 'normal' value may still hide reduced kidney function.
Low albumin reflects protein malabsorption and malnutrition; it also lowers total calcium.
Anemia from iron, folate, vitamin B12 and copper malabsorption; often mixed and may be macrocytic or microcytic.
Low MCV points to iron or copper deficiency; a high MCV points to B12 or folate deficiency.
Thrombocytosis can accompany iron deficiency; thrombocytopenia is rare and suggests another process.
Prolonged because of fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption; also seen with hepatic dysfunction from long-term parenteral nutrition.
Low after ileal resection, since B12 is absorbed in the terminal ileum.
Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency; ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and can be falsely normal with inflammation.
Rises in iron deficiency.
Mild elevation can reflect iodine or selenium deficiency; check free T4 if TSH is clearly high.
Nonspecific; a marked rise suggests an infectious or inflammatory complication such as catheter-related bloodstream infection or recurrent Crohn disease.
High specific gravity supports dehydration and prerenal azotemia.
From poor intake and malnutrition; not specific.

findings.finding: Prolonged QT interval from hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia
Flattened T waves and prominent U waves from hypokalemia
Atrial or ventricular ectopy and, when electrolytes are severely low, tachyarrhythmias

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected obstruction, abscess, fistula or recurrent Crohn disease

findings.text: Markedly shortened small bowel with surgical anastomoses and absent or resected ileocecal valve
Dilated fluid-filled bowel loops consistent with obstruction
Intra-abdominal abscess or inflammatory bowel wall changes suggesting recurrent Crohn disease
Pneumatosis or portal venous gas suggesting bowel ischemia
Multiple air-fluid levels and dilated loops suggesting obstruction

imaging.study: Upper gastrointestinal series with small bowel follow-through
imaging.preferred_when: Mapping residual bowel length and anatomy when surgery is being considered

findings.text: Short residual small bowel with rapid transit and loss of normal mucosal folds
Stricture or narrowed segment suggesting Crohn disease

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected Crohn disease or small bowel stricture without acute obstruction

findings.text: Bowel wall thickening and enhancement with skip lesions
Gallstones from fat malabsorption and altered enterohepatic circulation
Nonspecific; limited evaluation of the small bowel

imaging.preferred_when: Assessment of metabolic bone disease from calcium and vitamin D malabsorption

findings.text: Reduced bone mineral density (osteopenia or osteoporosis)

initial.why: Anemia and micronutrient deficiency are common; also screens for infection
Sodium, potassium, bicarbonate, BUN and creatinine show dehydration and electrolyte losses
Albumin, total protein and liver tests assess protein malabsorption and hepatic function
Hypomagnesemia is common and causes cramps and arrhythmia
Hypocalcemia from vitamin D and fat malabsorption
Terminal ileum is the site of B12 absorption and is often resected
Iron deficiency from malabsorption and chronic blood loss
Fat-soluble vitamin K malabsorption prolongs the INR
Thyroid disease can mimic or worsen weight loss and diarrhea
Assesses hydration and screens for urinary infection

initial.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
initial.why: Evaluates for obstruction, abscess, fistula or recurrent Crohn disease
initial.only_if: acute abdominal pain, distension or suspected complication

confirmatory.test: Upper gastrointestinal series with small bowel follow-through
confirmatory.why: Maps residual bowel length and anatomy, supporting the diagnosis and surgical planning
Defines residual bowel and excludes stricture or active Crohn disease when surgery is considered
confirmatory.only_if: Crohn disease or a stricture is suspected

supporting.why: Suggests an infectious or inflammatory complication when elevated
Rapid screen for obstruction when the abdomen is distended
Bedside assessment of bowel dilation and gallstones
supporting.only_if: right upper quadrant pain or suspected gallstones

supporting.why: Screens for metabolic bone disease from calcium and vitamin D malabsorption

not_indicated.why: No role in malabsorption or chronic diarrhea
Not needed unless pancreatitis is suspected
Only useful when bowel ischemia is suspected
Not part of the malabsorption workup; order only when pregnancy is possible and imaging or treatment depends on it
not_indicated.only_if: pregnancy is possible and imaging or treatment depends on it

decision_points: Confirm the diagnosis from surgical history, residual bowel length and malabsorption labs rather than from any single test
Assess fluid, electrolyte and micronutrient status before attributing symptoms to the short bowel itself
Image urgently when obstruction, ischemia, abscess or fistula is suspected
Pregnancy test before CT in anyone who could be pregnant

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic watery diarrhea, weight loss and bloating with micronutrient deficiency in a patient who has had abdominal surgery
differential.trigger: Diarrhea and weight loss with iron or folate deficiency, even without a clear surgical cause

history: Symptoms began before any bowel surgery
Long-standing diarrhea and weight loss rather than a clear postoperative change
Bloating and foul-smelling stools with a family history of celiac disease
exam: Signs of dermatitis herpetiformis or aphthous ulcers
labs: Positive tissue transglutaminase IgA with elevated total IgA
Iron and folate deficiency with normal B12
No severe sodium, potassium or bicarbonate losses
imaging: Small bowel biopsy showing villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia
Normal residual bowel length on small bowel follow-through

differential.name: Crohn disease
differential.why_considered: Recurrent diarrhea, weight loss and micronutrient deficiency in a patient who may have had multiple bowel resections for the same disease
differential.trigger: Diarrhea with fever, abdominal pain or perianal disease after prior resections

history: Symptoms recurring after a period of stability
exam: Perianal fistula, abscess or skin tags
Right lower quadrant tenderness or a palpable mass
imaging: Bowel wall thickening with skip lesions on CT or MR enterography

differential.name: Lactose intolerance
differential.why_considered: Bloating, gas and watery diarrhea after meals in a patient with malabsorption

history: Symptoms only after milk or dairy products
labs: Positive hydrogen breath test after lactose load

differential.name: Chronic mesenteric ischemia
differential.why_considered: Postprandial abdominal pain and weight loss in a patient with vascular risk factors or prior bowel infarction
differential.trigger: Severe postprandial pain with food fear and weight loss

history: Pain begins 15 to 30 minutes after eating and lasts hours
Fear of eating and progressive weight loss
History of atrial fibrillation, peripheral arterial disease or smoking
labs: Normal stool output and no high-output diarrhea
imaging: Celiac or superior mesenteric artery stenosis on CT angiography

differential.name: Bile acid malabsorption
differential.why_considered: Chronic watery diarrhea after ileal resection or cholecystectomy, often confused with short bowel syndrome

history: No significant weight loss or dehydration
imaging: Normal or near-normal residual bowel length

differential.name: Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth
differential.why_considered: Bloating, diarrhea and malabsorption in a patient with altered bowel anatomy or prior surgery

history: History of stricture, fistula or blind loop
labs: Positive hydrogen or methane breath test
imaging: Blind loop, stricture or fistula on small bowel follow-through

differential.name: Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency
differential.why_considered: Steatorrhea, weight loss and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency in a patient with malabsorption

history: Bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float
History of chronic pancreatitis, alcohol use or pancreatic surgery
exam: No surgical scars from bowel resection
labs: Low vitamin A, D, E and K levels
imaging: Pancreatic atrophy or calcifications on CT

differential.name: Hyperthyroidism
differential.why_considered: Weight loss, diarrhea and fatigue in a patient with chronic illness

exam: Tachycardia, tremor, goiter or lid lag
labs: Low TSH with elevated free T4
imaging: Diffuse or nodular thyroid uptake on scan

severity.mild: Residual small bowel is sufficient for oral nutrition; intermittent diarrhea and mild micronutrient deficiency without dehydration or significant weight loss
severity.moderate: Chronic diarrhea with weight loss and electrolyte abnormalities; requires oral rehydration, antidiarrheals and micronutrient supplementation, with occasional intravenous fluids
severity.severe: High-output stoma or diarrhea with dehydration, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and metabolic acidosis; requires parenteral nutrition or intravenous fluid support and frequent monitoring
severity.critical: Profound dehydration, shock, severe electrolyte derangement with arrhythmia, or sepsis from catheter-related bloodstream infection; life-threatening without urgent resuscitation

red_flags.meaning: Severe volume depletion or sepsis; needs urgent resuscitation

red_flags.finding: Stoma output over 2 liters per day
red_flags.meaning: High-output stoma with major fluid and electrolyte losses; risk of hypovolemia and hypokalemia
Severe electrolyte abnormality, dehydration or sepsis

red_flags.finding: Fever with chills in a patient with a central line
red_flags.meaning: Catheter-related bloodstream infection until proven otherwise

red_flags.finding: Absent or high-pitched bowel sounds with distension and vomiting
red_flags.meaning: Obstruction or ischemia; needs urgent imaging
Arrhythmia from severe hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia

complications.name: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
clues: Erythema or tenderness at the catheter site

complications.name: Cholelithiasis
clues: Right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals

complications.name: Metabolic bone disease
clues: Reduced bone mineral density on DXA

complications.name: Micronutrient deficiency (B12, folate, iron, copper, zinc, vitamins A, D, E, K)

special_populations.differences: Most cases follow necrotizing enterocolitis or congenital anomalies; growth failure is the main concern and parenteral nutrition is often required to support growth.
Present with failure to thrive, dehydration and poor feeding; small residual bowel length and rapid transit make fluid and electrolyte management especially difficult.
Blunted thirst and comorbidities increase the risk of severe dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities; kidney function may decline with chronic volume depletion.
Higher nutritional demands and nausea and vomiting of pregnancy worsen malabsorption; close monitoring of weight, electrolytes and micronutrients is needed, and parenteral nutrition may be required.
Reduced ability to concentrate urine and excrete potassium makes volume and electrolyte management harder; creatinine may be falsely low when muscle mass is depleted.
Diarrhea and erratic absorption make glucose control difficult; carbohydrate malabsorption and altered enterohepatic circulation can cause both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia.

key_questions.question: Have you ever had surgery on your intestines? What was removed, and how much bowel is left?
key_questions.looking_for: Extensive small bowel resection, residual length under about 200 cm, and whether the ileocecal valve or colon was removed

key_questions.question: How many stools or how much stoma output do you have in a day?
key_questions.looking_for: High-volume watery diarrhea or stoma output, often over 2 liters per day, indicating major fluid and electrolyte losses

key_questions.question: How much weight have you lost, and over what period?
key_questions.looking_for: Significant unintentional weight loss despite eating, pointing to malabsorption rather than poor intake

key_questions.question: Are you able to eat and drink enough, and does eating make the diarrhea worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms worsening after meals, especially large, high-fat or high-sugar meals, and fluids taken with meals

key_questions.question: Do you get intravenous fluids or nutrition through a line or port?
key_questions.looking_for: Dependence on parenteral nutrition or IV fluids, and presence of a central line that could become infected

key_questions.question: What antidiarrheal or acid-reducing medicines do you take, and do they help?
key_questions.looking_for: Use of loperamide, octreotide, proton pump inhibitors or prednisone, and whether symptoms respond

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, or redness or pain at your line site?
key_questions.looking_for: Catheter-related bloodstream infection, which is a life-threatening complication in patients on parenteral nutrition

key_questions.question: Have you had cramping abdominal pain, vomiting or abdominal swelling?
key_questions.looking_for: Small bowel obstruction from adhesions or a stricture, which needs urgent imaging

key_questions.question: Do you feel weak, dizzy on standing, or have muscle cramps or palpitations?
key_questions.looking_for: Dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities such as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia or hypocalcemia

key_questions.question: Any tingling or numbness in your hands and feet, or trouble with balance?
key_questions.looking_for: Vitamin B12 or copper deficiency neuropathy after ileal resection

key_questions.question: Any easy bruising, bleeding gums or night vision problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (A, D, E, K) from fat malabsorption

key_questions.question: Any bone pain or history of fractures?
key_questions.looking_for: Metabolic bone disease from calcium and vitamin D malabsorption

key_questions.question: Any blood in your stool, fever or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent Crohn disease or another inflammatory process rather than short bowel syndrome alone

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of Crohn disease, mesenteric ischemia or necrotizing enterocolitis?
key_questions.looking_for: The underlying cause of the resection and risk of recurrent disease

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have celiac disease or inflammatory bowel disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative or coexisting causes of malabsorption

reasoning_points: Extensive small bowel resection leaving insufficient absorptive surface, often with loss of the ileocecal valve or colon
Chronic high-volume watery diarrhea or stoma output with weight loss despite adequate intake
Signs of dehydration and malnutrition on exam, including surgical scars, temporal wasting and reduced muscle bulk
Electrolyte abnormalities such as hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Micronutrient deficiencies including low B12 after ileal resection, iron and folate deficiency, and prolonged INR from vitamin K malabsorption
Imaging or surgical history confirming markedly shortened residual small bowel
Exclusion of look-alikes such as celiac disease, Crohn disease, lactose intolerance, bile acid malabsorption and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency

easy: Clear history of massive small bowel resection with a known residual length under 200 cm
Obvious high-output diarrhea or stoma output with weight loss
Visible laparotomy scars and signs of malnutrition on exam
Typical electrolyte and micronutrient abnormalities on labs
medium: Patient with prior ileal resection and diarrhea but preserved nutrition, requiring distinction from bile acid malabsorption
Crohn disease patient with multiple resections where recurrent disease must be excluded
Mild presentation with intermittent diarrhea and isolated micronutrient deficiency
Older adult with dehydration and electrolyte abnormalities but less obvious diarrhea
hard: Infant after necrotizing enterocolitis presenting with failure to thrive and dehydration rather than classic diarrhea
Patient with a central line and fever where catheter-related bloodstream infection is the immediate threat
Presentation with obstruction or fistula rather than malabsorption as the chief problem
Coexisting celiac disease or pancreatic insufficiency masking or mimicking short bowel syndrome
Normal or near-normal appearing labs early in the course despite significant malabsorption
